events.title: U.S. and Iran open indirect nuclear negotiations mediated by Oman
events.summary: The United States and Iran open a new round of indirect nuclear negotiations mediated by Oman.
events.intro: Muscat reopened a negotiating channel after the previous year's war, without producing a nuclear agreement.
events.context: Oman used separate consultations to establish whether Washington and Tehran could resume sustained negotiations. The meeting was as much about restoring a workable diplomatic process as about resolving enrichment: officials left to consult their capitals rather than announce agreed technical limits.
details: Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi met separately with Iran's Abbas Araghchi and the American delegation of Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Oman's official account described work to clarify positions and establish conditions for further diplomatic and technical discussions. Araghchi also characterised the atmosphere positively, but the next meeting was not fixed in that announcement.

The talks took place under visible military pressure. AP reported the unusual participation of CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper and the presence of American naval forces in the region. Those circumstances made the restored channel consequential, but favourable descriptions of a first round were not evidence that either side had settled the central nuclear dispute.

events.title: Senior U.S. and Iranian delegations resume negotiations in Geneva
events.summary: Senior U.S. and Iranian delegations resume negotiations in Geneva.
events.intro: A set of negotiating principles was a basis for drafting, not a completed bargain over Iran's nuclear programme.
events.context: Araghchi's account of the Geneva round drew a clear line between agreeing how to negotiate and agreeing the final terms. Each side still needed to prepare text, exchange proposals and decide when to meet again.
details: After the Omani-mediated discussions in Geneva, Araghchi said the delegations had found a general understanding on guiding principles. He presented those principles as the basis for future drafting, while stressing that differences remained. Oman's mediator likewise reported progress on shared objectives and technical questions.

The proposed next step was for the parties to prepare and exchange written drafts before fixing another round. Araghchi did not announce a completed agreement or an immediate implementation schedule. The historical importance of the meeting lies in the move toward negotiating text; it does not support treating Iran's enrichment limits, inspections or sanctions relief as already settled.

events.summary: Trump says Iran has roughly 10–15 days to reach a meaningful nuclear agreement, otherwise bad things will happen. This is the first clear pre-war clock.
events.intro: Washington attached a short political clock to negotiations that had not yet produced agreed text.
events.context: Trump's warning sharpened the contrast between reported diplomatic progress and the American military buildup. His changing formulation—initially about ten days and then ten to fifteen—was an approximate decision window, not a published agreement with an enforceable expiry time.
details: At the Board of Peace meeting in Washington, Trump warned of consequences if Iran failed to reach what he considered a meaningful nuclear agreement. Asked later aboard Air Force One, he described ten to fifteen days as the maximum period. The warning followed the Geneva round, where the parties had only begun moving toward draft proposals.

Reuters reported the threat alongside growing U.S. military deployments and Iranian warnings that American bases could be attacked in response to a strike. These were reciprocal deterrent statements during an unfinished negotiation. Nothing in the announcement establishes that Washington had already issued an irrevocable order to begin war on a particular date.
events.editor_note: First explicit countdown immediately preceding the 2026 war.

relationships.label: Countdown precedes attack
relationships.summary: Trump's 19 February deadline statement was followed nine days later by coordinated U.S.-Israeli attacks. The sequence does not by itself establish when the attack decision was made.

events.title: Oman reports positive push in negotiations
events.summary: Oman's foreign minister announces that U.S.–Iran talks will resume in Geneva on 26 February and describes a positive push toward agreement. The announcement does not present a completed deal.
events.intro: Oman's announcement kept a third round on the calendar while avoiding any claim that a final deal existed.
events.context: The mediator identified Geneva as the venue for the next Thursday's talks and described a positive push toward agreement. Its optimism concerned the prospect of continued negotiation; it did not supply a signed framework or a detailed list of concessions.
details: Albusaidi announced that the next U.S.–Iran meeting would take place in Geneva on 26 February. The Omani statement connected that meeting to work on common objectives and technical issues. Coming after Trump's warning of a short deadline, a scheduled new round preserved an opportunity to turn preliminary understandings into negotiating text.

The scheduled round fell within the short window Trump had publicly allowed on 19 February. Oman was keeping the channel open and directing attention toward technical questions; it had not announced that either side had abandoned its central demands. Diplomatic optimism and military pressure were simultaneous features of this phase, not mutually exclusive descriptions of whether talks could continue.

events.intro: The third round was held in Geneva; Oman supplied the mediation, not the meeting's location.
events.context: Albusaidi's closing statement kept both political consultations and technical work alive. It announced further work in Vienna with the IAEA the following week, indicating that important implementation questions still required specialist negotiation.
details: Oman described the third U.S.–Iran round in Geneva as making significant progress. The delegations were to return to their capitals for consultations before continuing, while technical-level discussions were planned in Vienna. Oman's foreign ministry thanked the Swiss hosts and the International Atomic Energy Agency, leaving little ambiguity about where the political round occurred.

The scheduled technical follow-up distinguished the mediator's encouraging assessment from an agreement ready to enter into force. Nuclear limits and verification arrangements still had to be translated into acceptable detail. The attacks two days later interrupted a process that the mediator publicly presented as continuing, rather than a negotiation it had formally declared exhausted.

events.context: On the eve of the attacks, the apparent opening concerned whether Iran could enrich uranium without accumulating a usable stockpile and under extensive verification. That was distinct from Washington's demand that Iran cease producing nuclear fuel altogether.

In an interview reported by PBS, he described Iranian acceptance of no accumulation of enriched material and broad verification, including an American role. These were the mediator's account of an emerging understanding, not a jointly published U.S.–Iran agreement.

PBS explicitly distinguished the reported stockpile proposal from stopping enrichment entirely. Trump, meanwhile, said he was unhappy with Iran's negotiating position and insisted it should not create nuclear fuel. The remaining gap therefore concerned the permitted activity as well as the amount retained. Technical talks were still being planned when military action began the next day.

events.title: United States and Israel launch coordinated attacks on Iran
events.summary: The United States and Israel launch coordinated large-scale attacks on Iran, beginning the present war. Targets include leadership, missile, air-defence and other military sites.
events.intro: The opening campaign combined attacks on Iran's leadership with a much wider attempt to damage its military capacity.
events.context: The war began while an Omani-mediated negotiating process was still publicly active. Its opening attacks reached beyond nuclear installations to leadership, air-defence, missile and naval targets, immediately raising questions about whether the objective was coercion, military degradation or the overthrow of Iran's government.
details: Israeli and American attacks began on the morning of 28 February in Iran, with explosions reported in Tehran and other cities. Trump urged Iranians to take control of their government, while Iran condemned the attack and began responding across the region. The attacks therefore opened a direct interstate war rather than another isolated exchange confined to one military installation.

CENTCOM's first-day fact sheet described Operation Epic Fury as striking command centres, Revolutionary Guard facilities, air defences, launch sites and naval assets. Its figure of more than 1,000 targets in the first 24 hours is an American operational claim, not an independently audited inventory of destroyed facilities. The breadth of the stated target set nevertheless shows how much wider the campaign was than a single strike on enrichment equipment.

The timing broke sharply with the mediator's account of diplomacy: technical discussions had been planned after the Geneva round. That does not establish that a final agreement was imminent, but it does mean negotiation had not been publicly declared finished. Iran's immediate retaliation and the killing of its supreme leader created escalation and succession problems from the war's first day.

events.title: Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei killed
events.summary: Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei is killed during the opening attacks. Iranian state media subsequently confirms his death. Other senior political and military officials are also killed.
events.intro: The death of a leader in office since 1989 produced an immediate succession crisis, not evidence that Iran's institutions had collapsed.
events.context: Khamenei's authority connected the supreme leader's office, the Revolutionary Guards and Iran's regional strategy. Killing him in the opening attacks removed a central decision-maker while leaving the institutions capable of retaliation and succession in place.
details: Iranian state media confirmed Khamenei's death early on 1 March, following the attacks of 28 February. The distinction between the strike date and the confirmation date matters: reports and official claims circulated before the Iranian acknowledgement. Reuters' biographical account described an 86-year-old leader whose tenure had shaped the state's response to domestic opposition and its confrontations abroad.

His death did not itself determine the successor or terminate Iran's military response. The immediate historical question was how the ruling institutions would preserve authority while under attack. The subsequent selection of his son Mojtaba was a separate decision, and should not be treated as an automatic legal inheritance or as proof that the bombing had removed the political system.

events.title: Iran launches immediate regional missile and drone retaliation
events.summary: Iran immediately launches missiles and drones toward Israel and U.S. or allied military facilities across the Gulf region.
events.intro: Gulf states hosting American forces became part of the opening exchange, with civilian consequences beyond the intended military targets.
events.context: Iran's response immediately widened the geographical scope of the war. Hosting U.S. facilities exposed Gulf countries to attacks and emergency restrictions even though those governments did not present themselves as participants in the initial bombing campaign.
details: Reporting on 28 February documented Iranian attacks across the Gulf alongside the strikes toward Israel. Bahrain said a service centre connected with the U.S. Fifth Fleet had been hit, and Reuters witnesses observed smoke near the base. In the United Arab Emirates, authorities reported a fatality, while Qatar instructed people to shelter.

Military facilities were central to Iran's stated targeting, but those claims do not establish where every missile or drone landed. Airspace restrictions, explosions around populated areas and disruption to travel were separate effects of the exchange. The evidence supports a regional retaliation campaign; it does not justify describing every damaged civilian site as a U.S. base or every impact as a successfully reached target.

events.title: Minab primary-school strike kills scores of children; investigations point to U.S. responsibility
events.summary: The Shajareh Tayyebeh primary-school complex in Minab is struck, killing boys, girls and adults. AP's July reconstruction cites 157 identified dead, including 123 children; Airwars retains a 157–168 civilian range. Investigations point toward U.S. responsibility, but a final public Pentagon determination was not independently located in this review.
events.intro: Independent investigations identified large numbers of children killed and evidence pointing to U.S. responsibility; the victim totals and formal findings require careful dating.
events.context: Later AP, Airwars and Sky investigations documented child and adult deaths, distinguished the school from adjoining military facilities, and examined evidence pointing to U.S. responsibility. Their casualty counts reflect different investigation dates and methods.
details: At Shajareh Tayyebeh primary school, staff began contacting families to collect children as news of the attacks spread. AP's July reconstruction described pupils, teachers and parents caught when the school was struck. The school had once belonged to a larger military compound but had been fenced off for more than a decade. That history is relevant to the targeting evidence; it is not evidence that the building was functioning as a military facility on 28 February.

The casualty accounts should not be collapsed into one purportedly final number. AP cited Airwars' identification of 157 dead, including 123 children aged 13 or younger and 34 adults. Airwars' case record retained a wider range of 157–168 civilian deaths. Sky's separate identification work documented both boys and girls and used a different count. These are different research snapshots and methods, not interchangeable tallies of confirmed children killed.

Visual and investigative reporting increasingly pointed to an American weapon and possible failures in identifying the school. AP reported on 1 July that the Pentagon's inquiry was largely complete but still under review; Sky's later investigation also concluded that the evidence pointed to the United States. Those findings are stronger than the opening day's uncertainty, but an independently located final public Pentagon determination is not available in this review. The distinction preserves accountability questions without presenting an unpublished official conclusion as established.

events.title: Iran sharply restricts shipping through the Strait of Hormuz
events.summary: Iran sharply restricts shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and begins enforcing control over vessel movements.
events.intro: Shipping contracted through threats, disrupted insurance and company decisions as well as direct Iranian enforcement.
events.context: Hormuz's disruption was not a simple switch between fully open and physically sealed. Warnings, attack risk and vessels waiting outside the passage could sharply reduce trade without every transit becoming impossible; later permission systems further complicated what reopening would mean.
details: As the war began, oil companies, traders and shipping operators suspended or reconsidered voyages through the Strait of Hormuz. Reuters reported vessels sheltering and governments advising shipping away from the affected waters. This commercial response began alongside Iranian warnings and attacks, rather than only after a single universally effective closure order.

ACLED's reconstruction places Revolutionary Guard threats on 28 February and 2 March within a developing effort to pressure the global energy market. The military risk extended beyond the narrow channel to ports, loading facilities and approaches in the Gulf. Consequently, a ship's ability to cross the strait did not necessarily establish that its whole voyage was safe.

The early disruption became central to later negotiations because restoring normal trade required more than political declarations. Operators needed reliable passage and acceptable risk, while Iran sought leverage from controlling movement. This explains why the March threats and April ceasefire announcements repeatedly returned to the waterway without immediately returning traffic to normal.

events.title: Hezbollah joins the 2026 war
events.summary: Hezbollah joins the war, firing toward Israel in response to the killing of Khamenei and Israeli attacks. Israel intensifies attacks in Lebanon.
events.intro: Renewed Hezbollah fire reopened a Lebanese front that the November 2024 ceasefire had never fully pacified.
events.context: Hezbollah presented its rocket and drone attack as retaliation for Khamenei's killing and continuing Israeli attacks. Israel's response brought heavy strikes and renewed displacement in Lebanon, exposing the gap between Hezbollah's regional commitments and Lebanese leaders' efforts to avoid another war.
details: Contemporaneous reports date Hezbollah's announced attack and the ensuing Israeli strikes to early 2 March. AFP described it as the group's first claimed attack since the November 2024 ceasefire. That ceasefire had not meant the absence of Israeli strikes or accusations that Hezbollah was rearming, so the new exchange followed a period of contested enforcement rather than undisturbed peace.

Reuters reported attacks on Beirut's southern suburbs and southern Lebanon, with the Lebanese health ministry reporting 31 deaths in the initial response. Roads filled with people leaving affected areas. The front's reopening mattered not only militarily: it placed communities already exposed to the previous war under renewed pressure and conflicted with the Lebanese government's desire to stay out of the U.S.–Iran confrontation.

events.intro: Air attacks and evacuation orders on 2 March were followed by an announced ground deployment on 3 March.
events.context: The expansion rapidly turned military warnings into mass movement by civilians. Southern villages, the Bekaa Valley and Beirut's southern suburbs were affected, adding to earlier displacement and the pressures on Lebanon's already strained humanitarian system.
details: UNHCR's 3 March briefing described evacuation warnings affecting 53 villages and growing displacement from several parts of Lebanon. Families were moving under bombardment and uncertainty about where they could safely remain. Its account is evidence of the humanitarian consequences, not a verification that every location named by the military contained a Hezbollah position.

Reports of the ground component are dated 3 March, when Israel described troops taking additional forward positions in southern Lebanon. The distinction prevents the timeline from compressing two days of escalation into a single ground offensive on 2 March. The air campaign, withdrawal from exposed areas and ground deployment formed a sequence, with civilian displacement already underway before all its military elements were announced.

events.title: Heavy Lebanon fighting continues as incidents affect Erbil
events.summary: Heavy Israel-Hezbollah fighting continues; meanwhile drone and missile incidents affect sites around Erbil as Iranian-aligned forces and U.S. assets across the region become part of the wider exchange.
events.intro: Incidents in Iraqi Kurdistan involved several locations and actors; they should not be collapsed into a single Iranian strike on a U.S. base.
events.context: The wider war reached communities and installations in Iraqi Kurdistan while fighting continued in Lebanon. Local reporting differentiated drone impacts near Choman, interceptions around Erbil and a separate incident near Sulaimani, with incomplete attribution and no uniform target picture.
details: Kurdistan24 reported drone strikes in the Choman area, including damage at a social-care directorate and near residences, with local officials reporting no human casualties. Rudaw separately described interceptions near Erbil and an incident around Sulaimani. The accounts differed in some incident counts, which is a reason to preserve the individual locations rather than manufacture one reconciled total.

An Iraqi armed group claimed responsibility for a sensitive target in the Sulaimani area, but a claim is not proof that the claimed target was struck. Nor does the presence of American facilities elsewhere establish that every incident was aimed at U.S. personnel. AFP also documented a broader pattern of drone and rocket incidents in Iraq. Together these reports establish regional spillover while leaving the authorship of particular attacks unevenly documented.

events.title: Iran announces Mojtaba Khamenei as new Supreme Leader
events.summary: Iranian authorities announce Mojtaba Khamenei as Iran's new Supreme Leader.
events.intro: The Assembly of Experts' choice emphasised continuity through a leader closely connected to the Revolutionary Guards.
events.context: Mojtaba Khamenei's succession joined a formal clerical selection process to an unusually dynastic outcome. His elevation signalled the survival of the ruling institutions after his father's death, without demonstrating how much effective control he could immediately exercise during wartime.
details: Iran's Assembly of Experts named Mojtaba Khamenei supreme leader in an announcement carried by state media. Reuters described him as a mid-ranking cleric with strong Revolutionary Guard connections and a longstanding position within his father's circle. The selection was therefore more than the emergence of an unknown religious figure; it elevated someone already connected to important centres of power.

Chatham House analyst Sanam Vakil interpreted the choice as a signal of continuity and resistance. Reuters also noted the tension between hereditary succession and the Islamic Republic's professed rejection of monarchy. Both points help explain the political meaning of the announcement, but neither proves complete institutional unity or provides an independent measure of the new leader's wartime command.

events.context: By 10 March, the scale of bombardment and its effects on residential areas challenged suggestions that operations were nearly over. The strikes came after Trump's suggestion that the war was close to complete had encouraged expectations of an early finish. Iran continued threatening regional energy flows and carrying out retaliatory attacks. The contrast is historically important: public forecasts, financial-market reactions and the actual pace of fighting were moving on different tracks, not documenting an agreed winding-down of operations.

Reuters described Kharg as handling around 90 percent of Iran's crude exports and reported that shipments were continuing. That makes the distinction between military facilities and export equipment essential. The episode threatened Iran's revenue without establishing that its oil trade had already been stopped. Trump's warning that the terminal could be attacked tied a possible next step to the maritime confrontation rather than proving that every subsequent Iranian attack was a direct reply to Kharg.

events.context: The school attack became an international accountability question as well as a wartime casualty event. events.summary: Iranian missiles hit Dimona and Arad late on 21 March, causing extensive damage and injuries in populated areas. Israel says its defences failed to intercept them. Reporting continues on 22 March; no strike on the nearby nuclear reactor is established.
events.intro: The strikes demonstrated an air-defence failure near sensitive sites, but did not establish that a nuclear facility was hit.
events.context: Missiles reached two southern Israeli towns despite attempted defences, causing extensive damage and injuries in civilian areas. The proximity of Dimona's nuclear complex and other military installations made target attribution especially sensitive: geography alone could not prove what Iran intended to strike.
details: Reuters dated the missile impacts in Dimona and Arad to late Saturday, 21 March, with damage assessments and rescue reporting continuing on 22 March. Israeli officials said the missiles had not been intercepted and that the failures were being investigated. Images and reporting described destroyed or badly damaged buildings and large numbers of injured people.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed attacks on military and security installations. That claim must remain separate from the observed impacts in populated towns. Neither the reporting checked here nor the towns' proximity to the Dimona reactor establishes a strike on the reactor itself. The event also coincided with threats over Gulf energy infrastructure, but those wider threats were not the same incident as the two missile impacts.

events.title: Trump gives Iran 48 hours to fully reopen Hormuz
events.summary: Trump gives Iran 48 hours to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz, threatening to obliterate Iranian power plants if it does not comply.
events.intro: Trump tied the safety of Iran's power grid to the reopening of a waterway essential to regional trade.
events.context: The threat created a short, specific coercive deadline after weeks of fighting. Iran answered by threatening regional energy and water infrastructure, so the threatened consequences extended to Gulf populations and facilities outside the countries conducting the initial attacks.
details: Trump demanded that Iran fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz within 48 hours or face attacks on its power plants. The statement was issued on the U.S. evening of 21 March and widely reported internationally on 22 March. Its original expiry therefore fell on the evening of 23 March in the United States, rather than two days after every article's publication date.

Reuters reported Iran threatening counterattacks against regional energy and water facilities if Washington struck. These were conditional threats on both sides, not confirmation that the entire infrastructure campaign had already been ordered or executed. Their interaction increased the risk that a maritime dispute would turn into reciprocal attacks with broad civilian effects.

The deadline was subsequently postponed on 23 March, before the threatened power-grid attacks were carried out under that ultimatum. This makes the episode a distinct stage in the diplomacy: a 48-hour threat followed by a five-day reprieve. It should not be merged with the later ten-day extension or April's final deadline.

events.title: Trump postpones threatened power-plant attacks for five days
events.summary: Before carrying out the threatened power-plant attacks, Trump announces a five-day postponement, claiming productive discussions with Iran. Tehran says there have been no direct negotiations with Washington.
events.intro: The reprieve applied to threatened power-grid attacks, while the existence and form of negotiations remained contested.
events.context: Trump's postponement changed the immediate deadline without resolving the war. Reports of Pakistani, Egyptian and Turkish mediation offered a way for indirect messages to coexist with Tehran's denial that it was negotiating directly with Washington.
details: With the 48-hour ultimatum nearing expiry, Trump delayed attacks on Iranian power infrastructure for five days and described recent discussions as productive. Iranian officials denied direct negotiations. Reuters reported intermediary activity involving Pakistan, Egypt and Turkey, a distinction that matters because indirect exchanges do not necessarily contradict a denial of face-to-face or direct talks.

Oil prices fell and equities recovered as traders reacted to the reduced immediate risk. That market response measured expectations, not a verified diplomatic breakthrough. The postponement did not amount to a comprehensive ceasefire: it held back one threatened category of attack while military operations and the dispute over Hormuz continued.

events.intro: Mediation was occurring alongside attacks, with the two sides far apart on what any settlement would require.
events.context: The energy-strike reprieve had not stopped the wider war. Pakistan's offer to host talks and reports of indirect exchanges existed alongside continuing attacks and Iranian demands for guarantees against a repeat campaign.
details: On 24 March, missile attacks and other military operations continued despite Trump's account of diplomatic progress. Pakistan publicly offered to host discussions. The gap between a limited postponement and a general cessation of fighting was therefore visible within a day: neither the statement nor the mediation effort had produced a region-wide operational halt.

Reuters, citing sources in Tehran, reported a harder Iranian negotiating position that included protection against renewed attacks, compensation and questions of control over Hormuz. Those were reported demands, not jointly agreed terms or necessarily a final published Iranian proposal. They help explain why exchanging messages through intermediaries could coexist with public denials of talks and continued battlefield pressure.

events.intro: The new endpoint was precise, but the pause still covered energy attacks rather than the whole campaign.
events.context: Trump set 6 April at 8 p.m. Eastern as the new limit for his energy-infrastructure reprieve. The announcement prolonged the space for diplomacy while leaving both the military confrontation and disagreement over proposed settlement terms unresolved.

Reuters reported the announcement while Iranian officials were reviewing an American proposal they criticised as one-sided.

The limited scope is crucial. A postponement of attacks on energy installations did not prohibit all strikes, suspend the maritime confrontation or establish accepted ceasefire terms. The announcement changed a presidential threat's timetable; it did not demonstrate Iranian acceptance of Washington's nuclear demands or establish that the two sides shared Trump's optimistic account of negotiations.

events.title: U.S. and Israeli strikes expand against Iranian infrastructure
events.summary: U.S. and Israeli strikes expand against Iranian military, industrial and nuclear-related infrastructure. Iran threatens reciprocal attacks against industrial targets and continues missile and drone retaliation.
events.intro: Industrial and nuclear-related sites were attacked during a period when energy attacks were supposedly on hold.
events.context: The target categories mattered: a steelworks containing industrial radiation gauges, a heavy-water installation and a uranium-processing site posed different hazards. Reporting an attack on a nuclear-related site did not itself establish a radiation release or the destruction of a weapons programme.
details: Reports on 27 March described strikes on Iranian steel plants and nuclear-related facilities, including Khondab and a facility in Yazd. AP reported that the IAEA said there was no nuclear material at Khondab, while accounts of the Yazd attack did not identify an off-site radiological release. These distinctions prevent the category 'nuclear-related' from becoming an unsupported claim of widespread contamination.

An Iranian regulatory report submitted to the IAEA's incident system described the 27 March Khuzestan steelworks attack. It said industrial cobalt-60 and caesium-137 gauges were present, one source was damaged and recovered, and monitoring found no radiological hazard. That is a documented regulator's report, not an independent IAEA attribution of the attack. Together the incidents show how the campaign reached industrial infrastructure while the separate energy-attack deadline remained postponed.

events.context: The comment concerned how long Washington expected its own operations to continue. It neither required an Iranian response by a specified hour nor established that the shipping crisis, nuclear dispute or regional fighting would be resolved when American attacks ended.
details: Speaking in the Oval Office on 31 March, Trump said the United States could leave the war in two or three weeks. Reuters' video record places the statement on that date, while international reporting continued into 1 April. It was an estimate of the remaining American campaign, not a negotiated end date accepted by Iran.

The distinction separates this entry from the succession of threats against power infrastructure. Those announcements demanded action by Tehran and specified consequences for non-compliance; this one offered an anticipated duration. Continuing attacks and uncertainty about the following day's presidential address gave no basis for treating the forecast as a ceasefire already in force.

Trump called the Iranian proposal significant but insufficient. The exchange helps explain why a new deadline did not mean the parties had agreed what compliance would entail: opening shipping, ending attacks and settling the nuclear question remained connected but distinct demands.

events.context: The president's warning that an entire civilisation could perish transformed the final hours of the deadline into a broader crisis of threatened destruction. details: On 7 April, Trump posted that a whole civilisation would die that night if Iran did not reach a deal. Reuters reported that two White House officials, speaking anonymously, described the language as a negotiating tactic rather than a threat of nuclear annihilation. Their explanation was the administration's account of intent, not a reason to erase the statement's severity. Conversely, the wording alone is not documentary evidence of an order to use nuclear weapons.

The subsequent ceasefire announcement came at 6:32 p.m. Eastern, before the 8 p.m. deadline. Preserving both developments prevents a misleading chronology in either direction: the threat was real public rhetoric, but the threatened deadline passed into a negotiated pause rather than the announced infrastructure assault.

events.title: Pakistan seeks two-week extension to Trump's deadline
events.summary: Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif asks Trump for a two-week extension or ceasefire while pressing Iran to reopen Hormuz. Pakistan's military leadership is involved in the mediation.
events.intro: Pakistan offered reciprocal breathing space: more time for diplomacy and a temporary reopening of Hormuz.
events.context: The proposal connected Washington's countdown with Tehran's control over shipping. By asking each side for a time-limited step, Pakistan sought an interval in which negotiations could occur without requiring an immediate final settlement of the war's underlying disputes.
details: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif publicly asked Trump to extend the deadline for two weeks and urged Iran to permit shipping through Hormuz for the same period. He also called for a ceasefire. Reuters reported that an Iranian official viewed the request positively and that the White House had received it.

At the moment of the appeal, a proposal was still a proposal: a White House response was pending. The eventual American announcement credited both Sharif and Field Marshal Asim Munir, but it should remain a separate event from Pakistan's earlier request. Reports dated 8 April in Pakistan described an appeal made during 7 April in the United States, creating a reporting-date boundary rather than two distinct initiatives.

events.title: Trump agrees to a two-week ceasefire and calls Iran’s ten-point proposal workable
events.summary: Less than 90 minutes before his deadline, Trump accepts a Pakistani-mediated two-week ceasefire conditional on the immediate and safe opening of the Strait of Hormuz. Trump credits Shehbaz Sharif and Field Marshal Asim Munir. Iran's foreign minister confirms a tentative understanding.
events.intro: The agreement suspended an imminent escalation but left its regional scope and the meaning of reopened shipping contested.
events.context: The ceasefire announcement substituted a two-week negotiating period for threatened attacks on Iran's power grid and bridges. It was a conditional understanding assembled through Pakistan, not a final peace treaty or American acceptance of every element in Iran's proposed settlement.
details: At 6:32 p.m. Eastern on 7 April, Trump announced a two-week suspension of bombing and attacks, conditioned on immediate safe passage through Hormuz. He credited Sharif and Munir. Iran's foreign minister said defensive operations would stop if attacks on Iran ceased and described passage through the strait in coordination with Iranian forces. Those statements overlapped without being identical guarantees of unrestricted traffic.

Trump described Iran's ten-point proposal as a workable basis for negotiations. That wording did not mean Washington had accepted all ten points, including disputed nuclear and regional demands. Pakistan invited delegations to further talks in Islamabad, leaving the central bargain to be negotiated during the pause rather than presenting it as already concluded.

The announcement also left an immediate disagreement over Lebanon. Israel accepted the Iran-related pause but did not treat its campaign against Hezbollah as covered in the same way. Reports of attacks after the announcement and competing victory claims show the limits of a political declaration's immediate effect. The pause was consequential, but it was not a verified halt to all regional warfare.

events.context: The Islamabad talks moved beyond shuttle messaging, but disagreement over Lebanon, frozen assets and the nuclear programme accompanied the delegations into the room. The meeting was described as the highest-level U.S.–Iran encounter since the 1979 revolution, not the first time American and Iranian officials had ever negotiated directly. Pakistan hosted while Lebanon's conflict and conditions for relief from financial restrictions remained contentious. The exceptional seniority of the delegations indicated political commitment to the process, but did not prove agreement on its agenda or eventual outcome.

events.context: After the failed Islamabad session, Washington translated diplomatic pressure into a maritime interdiction policy. Its notice applied to vessels of any nationality entering or leaving Iranian ports and coastal areas, including the Arabian Gulf and Gulf of Oman. The same notice said U.S. forces would not impede ships transiting Hormuz to and from non-Iranian ports. That was the declared American rule, not proof that every voyage remained safe or that its legality was accepted by Iran. It created a second form of maritime pressure alongside Iranian restrictions and set the context for later American boardings and seizures.

events.intro: The seizure followed American gunfire to disable the ship and occurred outside the narrow Strait of Hormuz.
events.context: The Touska operation put the American blockade into direct coercive practice. It connected a vessel's intended call at an Iranian port with interception in the north Arabian Sea, showing why the maritime confrontation could not be mapped only to the strait itself.
details: CENTCOM dated the operation to 19 April. It said USS Spruance intercepted the Iranian-flagged container ship while it was heading toward Bandar Abbas, issued warnings for six hours and then disabled propulsion with naval gunfire. Marines subsequently boarded and took custody. Those operational details come from the force conducting the interception.

USNI News independently reported the seizure and Iran's accusation that it violated the truce. The competing descriptions—blockade enforcement versus a ceasefire violation—were political and legal claims, not interchangeable facts. The ship's cargo, the warning sequence and the authority asserted for the action require separate evidence; none should be inferred solely from the fact that boarding occurred.

events.title: U.S. forces board tanker Tifani in the Indian Ocean
events.summary: U.S. forces board the sanctioned oil tanker Tifani in the Indian Ocean on 21 April, according to the Pentagon and contemporary reporting. The boarding is reported as occurring without incident; the vessel's flag status and the asserted legal basis remain contested details.
events.intro: The U.S. boarding expanded the confrontation into the Indian Ocean, far from Hormuz.
events.context: Tifani was an oil tanker associated with Iranian cargo, not an unidentified participant in a clash inside the strait. Reporting established the American boarding while leaving disputes over the vessel's flag status and the legal basis for intervention to be attributed.
details: On 21 April the Pentagon said American forces had boarded Tifani without incident in the Indian Ocean. AP reported an operation in the Bay of Bengal area; Reuters and maritime reporting placed the tanker near Sri Lanka on its eastward voyage. These accounts put the encounter well outside the Strait of Hormuz.

The Pentagon invoked a maritime right-of-visit framework and described the vessel as stateless, while published reporting gave inconsistent accounts of its flag status. Those distinctions matter to the claimed authority for boarding, but do not obscure who conducted it. The verified event is an American boarding of a sanctioned tanker; responsibility is not the same unresolved question as flag registration or legal justification.

events.title: Trump indefinitely extends U.S.-Iran ceasefire
events.summary: Trump extends the pause in attacks without a new fixed expiry date, saying it will continue until Iran submits a unified proposal and discussions conclude. He credits Pakistan's request and explicitly orders the U.S. blockade to remain in place.
events.intro: The open-ended extension suspended renewed attacks but explicitly kept the U.S. blockade in place.
events.context: Trump's decision reduced the immediate risk of resumed bombing without creating an agreed permanent peace. Its endpoint depended on a further Iranian proposal and the completion of discussions, so 'indefinite' described the absence of a fixed date rather than an unconditional mutual settlement.
details: Trump announced that he would continue the ceasefire following a request from Pakistan and wait for what he described as a unified Iranian proposal. He said the pause would last until that proposal had been considered and discussions concluded. The announcement came as the original two-week window approached expiry and plans for further high-level talks were uncertain.

He also directed that the blockade continue. This separated the bombing pause from the coercive maritime campaign and helps explain why ship confrontations could persist during a proclaimed ceasefire. Reuters documented the American announcement; it did not establish that Iran had signed an identical open-ended extension or accepted Washington's account of divisions within its leadership.
events.research_note: The extension and continuing-blockade instruction were corroborated. Claims about a fractured Iranian leadership are attributed to Trump; a mutually signed indefinite ceasefire was not located.

revisions.reason: The statement sets procedural conditions and maintains the blockade; it does not announce an unconditional permanent peace or establish that Iran signed the same open-ended extension.

previous.summary: Hours before the original two-week ceasefire would expire, Trump extends it indefinitely to allow negotiations to continue.

events.title: Vance’s return to Pakistan is postponed as Iran leaves talks unconfirmed
events.summary: A U.S. official tells AP that JD Vance’s planned return to Islamabad has been put on hold. Pakistan says Iran has not confirmed attendance; this is a postponed trip, not a meeting Vance attended without Iranian negotiators.
events.intro: A planned second Islamabad round failed to become an actual meeting as the ceasefire approached its deadline.
events.context: The dispute concerned the conditions for negotiations as well as the negotiating terms. Reuters’ preceding-day account described the U.S. blockade as an obstacle to Iran’s participation, while Pakistani officials were still trying to obtain agreement to return.
details: AP reported on 21 April that Vance remained in Washington and that his trip had been called off for the time being, citing a U.S. official who cautioned that plans could change. Witkoff and Kushner were expected in Washington for consultations. Pakistan’s information minister said Tehran had not formally confirmed a delegation.

Earlier reports that the sides might travel were expressions of expectation, not confirmation that talks occurred. Reuters had described Iran as considering participation without a final decision. Read alongside the existing 11–12 April meeting and 21 April ceasefire-extension records, this milestone separates the failed attempt to reconvene from both the first negotiating round and the decision to keep the truce in place.

events.title: IRGC fires on and seizes commercial vessels
events.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say they seized MSC Francesca and Epaminondas amid firing incidents in Hormuz. MSC Francesca's capture is separately corroborated, while Epaminondas's operator confirms an attack and boarding; the full detention details remain less clear. A third ship, Euphoria, is reported fired on before continuing its voyage.
events.intro: Ship operators and maritime authorities corroborated attacks, but not every detail of the Revolutionary Guards' seizure account.
events.context: The confrontations showed that a political bombing pause had not normalised commercial passage. Iran's account of navigation violations conflicted with reports from ship operators about permissions and warnings, making the circumstances of each vessel essential.
details: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they had seized MSC Francesca and Epaminondas. Reuters reported separate confirmation of MSC Francesca's capture from Montenegro's maritime authorities, which said the crew members concerned were safe. Epaminondas's operator confirmed an attack and boarding, including damage to the bridge, while the full detention picture remained less clear in contemporaneous accounts.

The captain's account that the ship had permission and received no warning conflicted with Iranian allegations about navigation requirements. A third vessel, Euphoria, was also reported fired on but continued its voyage. Treating these as one identical seizure would erase important differences: being approached, damaged, boarded and detained are distinct events with different evidentiary support.

events.title: Israel-Lebanon ceasefire arrangement extended
events.summary: The separate Israel-Lebanon ceasefire arrangement is extended by roughly three weeks following negotiations in Washington.
events.intro: The Washington extension was negotiated by states while Hezbollah remained outside the meeting.
events.context: The separate Lebanon arrangement was extended amid continuing violence and disagreement over Israeli positions and Hezbollah's weapons. Its announcement should not be mistaken for full implementation on the ground or folded into the distinct U.S.–Iran ceasefire.
details: Trump announced a three-week extension after meeting Israeli and Lebanese representatives in Washington. Reuters identified ambassadors Yechiel Leiter and Nada Moawad among the participants. The extension followed an initial ten-day ceasefire that began on 17 April, rather than creating the first pause in the Lebanon fighting.

Hezbollah was not represented and opposed the process. Lebanon sought Israeli withdrawal and resolution of outstanding border and prisoner issues, while Israel emphasised disarmament and continued holding forward positions. These different objectives explain why the extension could be diplomatically significant while attacks and accusations of violations continued. The announcement established a state-level arrangement, not proof that all armed actors had accepted or implemented it.

events.title: Trump cancels Witkoff and Kushner’s trip to Islamabad
events.summary: Trump calls off a planned Pakistan visit by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Iran’s foreign minister had held talks with Pakistani leaders, but Tehran had said no direct meeting with the U.S. was scheduled.
events.intro: The cancelled envoys’ visit was another missed opening after the first Islamabad talks, not a second completed negotiating round.
events.context: The two sides were communicating through Pakistan without agreeing on a direct encounter. Araghchi’s meetings with the hosts and the proposed U.S. visit should therefore be distinguished from a confirmed U.S.–Iran appointment.
details: In recorded remarks on 25 April, Trump said he had decided not to send the envoys, citing the lengthy journey and an Iranian proposal he considered inadequate. He also claimed a better proposal arrived shortly after the cancellation. The transcript establishes what he said and the decision he announced; it does not authenticate the contents or timing of an unpublished Iranian offer.

RFE/RL reported that Araghchi met Pakistani leaders before continuing his regional diplomacy, and that Iran’s foreign ministry had already ruled out a scheduled direct meeting with the Americans. The episode illustrates the difference between a mediator carrying proposals and all parties agreeing to sit together. It also prevents later retellings from turning a cancelled flight into a meeting at which Iranian diplomats simply failed to appear.

events.title: UAE reports Iranian attacks affecting Fujairah
events.summary: The UAE attributes missile and drone attacks to Iran and reports a fire at the Fujairah Oil Industry Zone. Three Indian nationals are reported injured; the precise attack attribution is not independently established.
events.context: Fujairah's oil infrastructure became part of the confrontation surrounding the U.S. effort to move ships through Hormuz. The reported damage was at the Fujairah Oil Industry Zone; describing it simply as a refinery fire overstates the facility identification available in the contemporary report.
details: UAE authorities said a drone attack started a fire in the industrial zone and moderately injured three Indian nationals. The same day's missile alert was a separate account: the defence ministry said three incoming missiles were intercepted and another fell into the sea. These reports should not be collapsed into a single weapon striking a refinery.

The UAE attributed the attacks to Iran. That attribution was reported by Reuters, but the account did not provide independent launch-site verification. Iran's Revolutionary Guards also publicised an expanded maritime-control area reaching toward the UAE coast, placing the incident within a wider dispute over how far Iran could enforce restrictions on shipping.
events.research_note: Contemporaneous Reuters search-index text checked; the publisher page returned an access error on direct opening. The occurrence, injuries and Iranian attribution are UAE reports. No independent damage survey or weapon-origin finding was located. A proposed summary amendment replaces 'refinery' with the documented oil-industry zone.

revisions.reason: Reuters identifies the oil-industry zone, not a specifically verified refinery, and attributes the attack account to UAE authorities.

events.title: Trump pauses Project Freedom Hormuz escort operation
events.summary: Trump pauses the active Project Freedom shipping-escort operation, launched on 4 May, while keeping the separate U.S. blockade of Iranian ports in force.
events.context: Project Freedom had already begun escorting shipping when Trump suspended it. The pause therefore interrupted an active operation, while leaving the separate U.S. blockade of Iranian ports in place.
details: The escort initiative began on 4 May. Trump said the following evening that it would be paused briefly to test whether negotiations could produce an agreement. Maersk had confirmed that the U.S.-flagged Alliance Fairfax left the Gulf under American escort, providing a concrete example of the operation before its suspension.

American officials were simultaneously trying to distinguish protection of commercial shipping from a return to the larger bombing campaign. Marco Rubio said the objectives of Operation Epic Fury had been achieved, while the military described recent Iranian attacks as below the threshold for renewed major combat. Neither formulation amounted to an agreed settlement of the competing blockades.
events.research_note: Reuters article opened and read. Corrects the base summary's description of an operation that was merely 'planned'. Trump's assessment of negotiating progress remains his assessment; the escort pause did not terminate the naval blockade.

revisions.reason: The operation had begun and a Maersk vessel had transited under escort; 'planned' is inaccurate.

previous.summary: Trump pauses the planned U.S. Project Freedom Hormuz escort operation while negotiations continue.

events.title: U.S. and Iranian forces exchange fire near Hormuz
events.summary: U.S. and Iranian forces exchange fire near the Strait. Iran says U.S. forces attacked ships and Qeshm; CENTCOM describes its actions as defensive.
events.context: The exchange exposed the gap between maintaining a ceasefire politically and avoiding combat at sea. Both governments described the other as the initiator, and Trump nevertheless insisted that the truce remained in force.
details: Contemporary Reuters reporting dates the fighting to Thursday, 7 May, although the article and video package were updated on 8 May. CENTCOM said Iranian missiles, drones and small boats attacked three U.S. destroyers without hitting them, and that American forces then struck missile and drone sites.

Iran's military gave a different sequence: it said U.S. forces first attacked an Iranian tanker, another vessel and civilian coastal areas, including Qeshm. Iranian claims of substantial damage to American assets were contradicted by CENTCOM. The exchange occurred while Washington awaited Iran's response to a proposed negotiating framework, leaving both sides an incentive to avoid declaring the ceasefire dead.
events.research_note: Reuters report and video transcript checked. The fighting is described as Thursday, 7 May, and the report was updated on 8 May. A precise London event hour was not established, so the proposed correction uses a 7–8 May overnight range. Initiation, civilian targeting and damage remain disputed.

revisions.reason: Reuters places the fighting on Thursday, 7 May, with reporting updated on 8 May. Because a precise London event hour was not established, a 7–8 May range is more conservative than replacing one single-day assertion with another.

events.title: Israeli strikes in Lebanon kill at least two dozen, according to Lebanese authorities
events.summary: Israeli strikes in Lebanon kill at least two dozen people according to Lebanese authorities, adding pressure to the separate Israel-Lebanon ceasefire.
events.context: The Lebanon ceasefire was being tested by continuing lethal strikes even while U.S.–Iran diplomacy focused on Hormuz. Lebanese leaders sought American pressure on Israel, and Tehran was also pressing for Lebanon's security to be included in a broader settlement.
details: The initial at-least-24 toll referred to Saturday 9 May, although the article appeared on 10 May. AP also described vehicle strikes near Beirut and attacks in the south, demonstrating that distinct incidents and reporting windows lay behind the broader casualty coverage.

Reuters subsequently reported President Joseph Aoun's appeal for Washington to restrain Israeli strikes and demolitions. Lebanese health authorities put deaths over the preceding three days at 74. That wider toll illustrates the pressure on the April truce, but it is a different reporting window from the Saturday count and does not independently resolve the final total for this entry.

events.title: Further shipping incidents occur off Oman and Fujairah
events.summary: A livestock vessel sinks after an attack off Oman on 13 May. On 14 May, an unauthorised boarding is reported northeast of Fujairah, with the vessel heading toward Iranian waters; the incidents have different attribution evidence.
events.context: These were two different maritime incidents on consecutive days, not a single attack. Their geography also matters: both occurred outside the narrowest part of Hormuz, extending insecurity into the Gulf of Oman.
details: Reuters reported that an Indian vessel carrying livestock from Africa to the UAE sank off Oman on Wednesday, 13 May. The next day, UKMTO reported an unauthorised boarding of a vessel anchored northeast of Fujairah. The ledger's single-day heading obscures that sequence.

Two maritime-security sources tentatively identified the boarded ship as the Honduras-flagged Hui Chuan, a fishery research vessel. Vanguard relayed an operator account that Iranian personnel took control and that contact and position transmissions were lost. This identification and attribution were not equivalent to an independently witnessed seizure, and they should remain separate from the less clearly attributed sinking.
events.research_note: Contemporaneous Reuters text checked. Proposes a 13–14 May range. Vessel identification was tentative in the boarding report; no conclusive attribution of the livestock-vessel sinking was established in the material checked. The source's erroneous description of an exclusive economic zone is not reproduced.

revisions.reason: Reuters explicitly separates Wednesday's sinking from Thursday's boarding.

events.title: Israel and Lebanon extend ceasefire framework by 45 days
events.summary: Israel and Lebanon extend their ceasefire framework by another 45 days.
events.context: The 45-day extension preserved a diplomatic process without establishing that fighting had stopped. Washington's negotiations separated political discussions from security arrangements, while the truce's implementation remained contested on the ground.
details: The U.S. State Department announced the extension on Friday, 15 May, after two days of Israeli–Lebanese talks in Washington. It prolonged the ceasefire that had begun in April and was otherwise approaching expiry. Reports published on 16 May in other time zones account for the ledger's later date.

The extension followed repeated strikes and Lebanese complaints that the earlier ceasefire was not protecting communities in the south. Further political and security meetings were envisaged rather than a final peace treaty. Hezbollah's position and the state's ability to implement security commitments remained distinct questions from the consent of the two negotiating delegations.
events.research_note: The U.S. announcement is dated 15 May in Reuters; 16 May is the Australian publication date. The extension itself is corroborated, but an agreement to extend should not be coded as proof of complete battlefield compliance.

revisions.reason: The U.S. State Department announced the extension in Washington on Friday, 15 May; 16 May reflects publication in another time zone.

events.title: Trump threatens that nothing will be left if Iran refuses a deal
events.summary: Trump threatens that if Tehran does not agree to U.S. terms, nothing will be left of Iran. Unlike March and April, he does not attach a precise timer.
events.context: Trump's language combined a warning of destruction with pressure to accept a negotiated settlement. It supplied no measurable countdown and did not announce a specific military operation.
details: The archived presidential post is dated 17 May and warns that time is running out for Iran. Its importance is the escalation of public coercion during a diplomatic impasse, not the creation of another hour-by-hour ultimatum comparable to earlier deadlines.

Contemporaneous reporting placed the warning alongside regional concern over a drone incident near the UAE's Barakah nuclear plant. That proximity in the news cycle does not establish that Trump was responding to that incident, or that Iran launched the drone. The statement is evidence of U.S. presidential rhetoric, not of Iranian acceptance of terms or an agreed attack schedule.

events.title: Drone incident near Barakah nuclear power plant
events.summary: A drone incident occurs near the perimeter of the UAE's Barakah nuclear power plant. No injuries or radiation release are reported. UAE authorities do not definitively attribute the drone to Iran.
events.context: The reported fire involved an external generator near a nuclear-power complex, making the location alarming without establishing damage to a reactor. Nuclear-safety reporting and attribution of the attack are separate evidentiary questions.
details: UAE authorities reported a drone strike affecting a generator outside Barakah's inner perimeter. The IAEA said it had been informed that radiation levels remained normal, and the UAE regulator reported that essential systems were operating normally. No injuries or radioactive release were reported.

Those statements constrain what can responsibly be inferred from images or the phrase 'nuclear plant attack': they do not describe a reactor breach. The UAE initially investigated the drone's origin without a definitive public attribution to Iran. The incident occurred amid the broader U.S.–Iran standoff, but that context alone cannot identify who launched it.

events.title: Trump says planned attack has been postponed
events.summary: Trump says he has postponed an attack he says was planned for 19 May while discussions continue. Reuters could not independently determine whether preparations for the previously unannounced operation were under way.
events.context: The postponement was announced as leverage for diplomacy after Pakistan passed on a revised Iranian proposal. The existence of a fully prepared attack plan was not independently established.
details: Trump said he had deferred an attack intended for Tuesday, 19 May, while leaving forces ready to act if discussions failed. He presented the decision as a response to negotiations and appeals from regional leaders, rather than an unconditional cancellation of military options.

Reuters explicitly noted that the proposed attack had not previously been announced and that it could not determine whether preparations had actually been under way. The reliable event is therefore Trump's announcement on 18 May. Treating an operational strike as demonstrably scheduled and then cancelled would go beyond the source.

events.title: Trump says an agreement is largely negotiated
events.summary: Trump says an agreement is largely negotiated, subject to finalisation. No final agreement follows immediately.
events.context: The announcement signalled proximity to an interim memorandum, not a completed peace agreement. Its immediate emphasis on reopening Hormuz left major nuclear and implementation questions unresolved.
details: Trump described an agreement as largely negotiated after discussions involving regional leaders and Benjamin Netanyahu. Pakistani military chief Asim Munir was again involved in the Iranian diplomatic channel. These contacts helped explain the optimistic announcement but did not substitute for publication or signature of an agreed text.

The contemporaneous AP account noted the absence of detailed nuclear provisions from Trump's announcement. A memorandum still had to be finalised, and neither the statement nor the accompanying reporting established that shipping access had already been restored. Subsequent attacks should therefore be understood as occurring during an unfinished diplomatic process, not after an already implemented settlement.

events.summary: U.S. strikes on 25 May draw Iranian accusations of ceasefire violations and claims of attacks on U.S. aircraft. Another U.S. strike near Bandar Abbas is reported on 27 May; asserted threats and aircraft losses remain attributed.
events.context: This sequence began before the ledger's start date: U.S. strikes on 25 May drew Iranian accusations the following day, and another American strike was reported on 27 May. The ceasefire label survived despite successive tactical engagements.
details: Reuters reported Iranian condemnation on 26 May of American strikes carried out on Monday, 25 May. Iranian claims to have downed a U.S. drone and fired on another aircraft were part of that response. They should remain attributed rather than becoming independently verified aircraft losses.

A further U.S. strike reported on 27 May targeted a drone-related site near Bandar Abbas, according to an American official. The official said drones and their control equipment were being prepared for use. This was a U.S. account of the immediate threat, not an independent assessment; the sequence shows how alleged imminent attacks were repeatedly invoked while negotiations continued.

events.title: Israel conducts another major round of attacks in Lebanon
events.summary: Israel intensifies bombardment and ground operations in southern Lebanon on 26 May. Lebanese authorities report dozens killed, and expanded evacuation warnings follow on 27 May.
events.context: The escalation combined bombardment with expanded ground activity beyond Israel's existing security zone. It also widened displacement pressure shortly before another diplomatic meeting and during Eid al-Adha.
details: Reuters described more than 120 strikes on Tuesday, 26 May, citing a Lebanese security source. Lebanese authorities reported at least 31 deaths and 40 injuries in the subsequent account; a strike on Burj al-Shamali was among the reported incidents involving women and children. These are attributed contemporaneous totals, not a final independently reconciled casualty list.

On 27 May, the Israeli military issued a broad warning for residents in southern Lebanon to leave, while AP reported operations crossing the Litani River around Zawtar al-Sharqieh. The timing matters: the ledger's date captures the reporting and evacuation phase, but much of the bombardment it summarises had happened the previous day.

events.title: U.S. and Iran exchange attacks around Hormuz and Gulf bases
events.summary: The U.S. reports intercepting Iranian missiles and drones aimed toward Gulf states and Hormuz and strikes Iranian coastal radar installations. Iran says it retaliates against U.S. bases in Kuwait and Bahrain.
events.context: Coastal surveillance sites and Gulf-based air defences were central to this exchange. Each side framed its action as retaliation, while the available operational detail came predominantly from military statements.
details: U.S. officials said American forces intercepted four Iranian drones before striking radar sites at Goruk and Qeshm. CENTCOM subsequently reported seven ballistic missiles fired toward Kuwait and Bahrain: six were intercepted and one failed to reach its target, according to the command.

Iranian reporting placed strikes around Sirik and Qeshm early on 6 June local time, so the sequence crosses an overnight boundary. Reuters geolocated released footage to a coastal installation but could not independently establish when it was recorded. That distinction prevents military handout imagery from being treated as complete verification of either chronology or damage.

events.title: Trump says U.S. wants total victory within two weeks
events.summary: Trump says the U.S. wants total victory within the next two weeks and says Iran is prepared to concede extensively. This is not framed as a formal two-week deadline.
events.context: The two-week prediction came in domestic campaign remarks, not a diplomatic ultimatum delivered to Tehran. Trump connected the expected outcome to Iran's nuclear programme and a promised fall in oil prices.
details: In a telerally for South Carolina candidates Lindsey Graham and Pamela Evette, Trump said negotiations were under way and portrayed Iran as willing to concede extensively. The American Presidency Project transcript records his expectation of declaring victory over the next two weeks.

The setting and wording matter. This was an optimistic forecast to supporters on the eve of a primary, without a stated expiration hour, an agreed negotiating timetable or a specified consequence triggered on a particular day. Iran's purported readiness to concede was Trump's assertion, not a commitment independently verified in the transcript.

events.title: Iran announces full closure of the Strait of Hormuz
events.summary: Iran declares Hormuz closed and threatens vessels attempting unauthorised transit. CENTCOM disputes a complete closure and says commercial vessels continue to pass.
events.context: Iran's closure announcement was a threat to enforce its transit rules, not proof that every ship had stopped. The U.S. military publicly disputed the claimed closure and said commercial traffic continued.
details: Iran's joint military command threatened to fire on vessels attempting passage after renewed U.S. attacks. Iranian state reporting presented this as a full closure, while reports of firing on ships underscored the danger to operators unwilling to follow Tehran's procedures.

CENTCOM denied that the strait was closed and said ships were still transiting. The competing statements described a contested waterway in which legal claims, military control and actual traffic volumes were different questions. A declaration of closure should consequently be labelled as an Iranian official claim rather than a verified cessation of all navigation.
events.research_note: Iranian state announcement and the opened Reuters counter-account checked. The closure declaration is corroborated as a statement; total physical closure is not. Proposes 'official_claim' instead of an unqualified confirmed outcome.

events.title: U.S. and Iran exchange attacks around the Strait and Gulf infrastructure
events.summary: The United States and Iran exchange attacks around the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf infrastructure.
events.context: The June exchange expanded beyond coastal encounters into an overt campaign of military pressure on negotiations. American officials described strikes as a way to improve Washington's bargaining position; Iran answered with regional-base attack claims.
details: CENTCOM said a new operation hit surveillance, communications and air-defence targets after midnight in Tehran, completing several hours later. Iranian media reported explosions in southern ports and inland locations, while Bahrain reported warning sirens during the Iranian response.

Successive Iranian statements named different sets of targets, including Jordan and bases in Kuwait and Bahrain. Those cumulative announcements should not be merged into a verified list of facilities struck. Reuters' reporting establishes renewed exchanges and public military claims, but it does not independently confirm the announced target counts or battle damage.

events.title: Trump threatens Iranian energy infrastructure, then says he cancels planned attacks
events.summary: Trump threatens control of Iranian oil and gas infrastructure, then says a negotiating opening has led him to cancel planned attacks. Iran says mediators are active but nothing has been finalised.
events.context: The shift from threatening Iranian energy assets to announcing a negotiating opening occurred within hours. It demonstrated that escalation and suspension were being used together in U.S. public diplomacy.
details: Trump threatened a much more severe campaign and U.S. control over Iranian oil and gas infrastructure, including pressure around Kharg. Later, he said Iranian leaders had approved renewed talks and announced that planned attacks would not proceed.

Iran's Foreign Ministry acknowledged continuing work by mediators but said nothing had been finalised. That qualification is essential: a presidential declaration of a breakthrough was not joint confirmation of agreed terms. The episode belongs in the timeline as a change in announced U.S. posture, while the existence and scale of any cancelled operation remain distinct questions.

events.title: U.S. and Iran announce ceasefire and peace framework
events.summary: Trump announces that Washington and Tehran have reached a ceasefire and peace framework. Iran's deputy foreign minister confirms that a framework exists.
events.context: The framework announcement marked agreement to pursue an interim settlement while leaving the most contentious nuclear details open. American and Iranian descriptions already differed over what would happen to enriched uranium.
details: Trump and Iranian officials announced progress toward an agreement through Pakistani mediation. Contemporary reporting discussed a later signing ceremony and measures involving Hormuz access, frozen Iranian funds and restrictions on further nuclear expansion. The announcement date spans Sunday in the United States and early Monday in the region.

U.S. officials described removal or destruction of Iran's enriched material, whereas an Iranian official discussed dilution inside Iran. These were rival interpretations of unfinished arrangements, not interchangeable descriptions of a settled obligation. Continued Israeli activity in Lebanon also complicated a framework that Tehran wanted to extend beyond the U.S.–Iran front.

events.title: U.S. and Iran confirm the signed 14-point Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding
events.summary: Pakistan says the United States and Iran have signed the 14-point Islamabad memorandum and that it is effective on 17 June. The framework envisages a 60-day negotiating process, while the exact clock start and several implementation details remain unclear.
events.intro: The framework paired military de-escalation with maritime and economic concessions, but left the nuclear settlement, future shipping rules and implementation machinery to further negotiation.
events.context: The memorandum attempted to convert a fragile ceasefire into an exchange of commitments: reduced military pressure and economic restrictions for restored shipping and negotiations on a permanent settlement. Its immediate political significance was substantial, but several headline provisions depended on later agreements.
details: Pakistan's prime minister said both sides had signed and that the memorandum took effect on 17 June. AP reported uncertainty over the exact signature sequence and when the 60-day negotiating clock began. A planned ceremony was therefore not the same thing as the framework's legal or political starting point. The 17 June milestone is best described as public confirmation of signature and effect, not merely transmission of an unsigned proposal.

Reuters examined a 14-point draft that coupled a permanent end to military operations, including Lebanon, with sovereignty commitments and negotiations for a final deal. The draft envisaged restoration of shipping and an end to the U.S. blockade, economic relief, reconstruction support and eventual arrangements for sanctions and frozen assets. These were negotiated commitments and proposed mechanisms, not evidence that money had already been paid or navigation restored.

The U.S. officials' version read to reporters, described by ABC News, limited guaranteed toll-free passage to 60 days and left future shipping arrangements for discussion. Iran's enriched-uranium stockpile and longer-term nuclear restrictions also remained subjects for negotiation. Because the written signed text was not then publicly released in full, differences between the Reuters draft and the U.S. readout must remain visible rather than being combined into a falsely definitive treaty text.

The White House had said the previous evening that Vance was no longer departing as planned, while Iran had not committed to the visit. Iranian reporting tied attendance to implementation of the agreement, with continued Israeli operations in Lebanon a central grievance.

This was a Swiss follow-up to the Islamabad memorandum, not another trip to Pakistan. Both delegations were attempting to turn the memorandum into workable arrangements, while presenting different priorities in public. Iran stressed Lebanon and economic commitments; Vance spoke about nuclear issues, Lebanon and maritime access. details: Qatar and Pakistan’s joint statement described a High-Level Committee, working groups on nuclear and sanctions questions, and monitoring and dispute-resolution arrangements. It set out a 60-day path towards a permanent agreement, a communication line for Hormuz and a Lebanon conflict-management mechanism. These were agreed structures for further work, not proof of a final peace settlement.

Treasury announced General License X on 22 June; the instrument was dated 21 June. Reuters reported that the limited oil and related-product authorization ran to 21 August. The diplomatic readouts still diverged: Vance described progress on inspections and implementation, whereas Iran’s foreign ministry said nuclear issues had not yet been discussed and no new commitments made. events.title: Commercial vessel using Omani-approved route is struck
events.summary: A commercial vessel using an Omani-approved shipping route is struck off Oman. Washington blames Iran; Tehran argues that vessels outside approved procedures cannot be guaranteed safe passage.
events.context: One attack disrupted more than the voyage of a single ship: it prompted the International Maritime Organization to suspend a newly begun evacuation arrangement while safety guarantees were reassessed.
details: UKMTO reported a commercial vessel hit by a projectile near Oman. Sources speaking to Reuters identified the Singapore-flagged Ever Lovely; a security source considered a drone the likely weapon. Two U.S. officials blamed Iran, while Tehran's maritime authority warned that it would not guarantee passage outside its approved procedures.

The vessel was not itself part of the IMO-assisted programme. Nevertheless, the incident led the organisation to pause that initiative only two days after it began. The distinction is important: the attack exposed uncertainty over rival Iranian and Omani transit arrangements, rather than proving that a ship under a specific UN escort had been deliberately attacked.
